title: Calibration: aligning stated confidence with actual accuracy

videos.script: Ask a model how sure it is, and it gives you a number. Point nine, say. It looks like a probability. It is text the model wrote, like everything else in the answer. {{number}} This lesson asks whether that number means anything. Over seventy answers the model uses four numbers, and almost every answer says point eight or point nine. On one message it says point nine, and it is wrong. {{h03}} One mistake proves nothing about a confidence. So you group seventy answers by what they claimed, and count how often each group was right. {{bins}} That gives you the picture this topic is known for. Stated confidence along one side, accuracy up the other, and a diagonal where the two agree. Both big groups land below it, and close together. {{diagram}} Then you put a number on the gap, two ways. Saying the same number every time would have scored better. And a threshold chosen on the easy set promises perfect answers. On the hard set it does worse than no threshold at all. {{threshold}} By the end you know how to measure a stated confidence, and why you never simply trust one. {{close}}
